Use the complex field $\mathbb C$ with conjugation $z\mapsto\overline z$. Fix an integer $N\ge1$. Let $S=\mathbb C^2$ have standard basis $s_1,s_2$. For a complex vector space $W$, its conjugate vector space $\overline W$ consists of symbols $\overline w$ for $w\in W$, with addition $\overline w+\overline v=\overline{w+v}$ and scalar action $\lambda\overline w=\overline{\overline\lambda w}$. Set $\dot S=\overline S$ with dotted basis $\dot s_{\dot1}=\overline{s_1}$ and $\dot s_{\dot2}=\overline{s_2}$. Let $F=\mathbb C^N$ have standard basis $f_1,\ldots,f_N$, and let $F^*$ be its complex-linear dual with dual basis $f^1,\ldots,f^N$ and scalar action $(\lambda\ell)(v)=\lambda\ell(v)$. All tensor products are over $\mathbb C$, with scalar action $\lambda(v\otimes w)=(\lambda v)\otimes w=v\otimes(\lambda w)$ and product bases formed from the displayed bases. Define $\Lambda^2F=(F\otimes_{\mathbb C}F)/\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{v\otimes v:v\in F\}$; its basis is $f_I\wedge f_J$ for $1\le I<J\le N$, with quotient scalar action. Its conjugate $\overline{\Lambda^2F}$ has basis $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ and the conjugate scalar action just defined. For $N=1$ these exterior-square spaces are zero. In the displayed bases, $\mathfrak{sl}(S)=\{A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(S):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$ and $\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)=\{B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\dot S):\operatorname{tr}B=0\}$. Put $\epsilon_{12}=\epsilon_{\dot1\dot2}=1$ and $\epsilon_{21}=\epsilon_{\dot2\dot1}=-1$, with zero diagonal. The complex even space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar0}=\bigl(\mathfrak{sl}(S)\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)\bigr)\oplus V\oplus C_N,\qquad V=S\otimes\dot S,\qquad C_N=\Lambda^2F\oplus\overline{\Lambda^2F}.$$

Write $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=s_\alpha\otimes\dot s_{\dot\beta}$ for the basis of $V$. The listed central generators form a basis of $C_N$: $Z^{IJ}$ corresponds to $f_I\wedge f_J$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ to $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ for $1\le I<J\le N$; extend them by antisymmetry in the flavor indices and set their diagonal entries to zero. The complex odd space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar1}=(S\otimes F)\oplus(\dot S\otimes F^*),$$

with basis $Q^I_\alpha=s_\alpha\otimes f_I$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=\dot s_{\dot\alpha}\otimes f^I$. A homogeneous vector has parity $|x|\in\{0,1\}$. The bracket is complex-bilinear, preserves parity, and obeys $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$. Its complete nonzero table, apart from the graded-skew consequences, is

$$[ (A,B),(A',B') ]=([A,A'],[B,B']),\qquad [(A,B),T]= (A\otimes I+I\otimes B)T,$$

$$[(A,B),Q^I_\alpha]=A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}Q^I_\gamma,\qquad [(A,B),\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}]=B^{\dot\gamma}{}_{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\gamma I},$$

Here $A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}$ is the entry in row $\gamma$, column $\alpha$, so $As_\alpha=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}s_\gamma$; dotted entries use the same convention. Thus on the translation basis the tensor action is $[(A,B),T_{\alpha\dot\beta}]=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}T_{\gamma\dot\beta}+\sum_{\dot\gamma}B^{\dot\gamma}{}_{\dot\beta}T_{\alpha\dot\gamma}$.

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\delta^I{}_J T_{\alpha\dot\beta},\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

All other brackets vanish: $V$ and $C_N$ are abelian, $C_N$ is central, and $V$ brackets trivially with the odd space. The two antisymmetric factors in each equal-chirality odd bracket make that bracket symmetric in the combined spinor-flavor labels. The Lie-superalgebra and real-form properties are established by the local Jacobi result.

Define a conjugate-linear involution $*$ on the generators by

$$ (A,B)^*=(-\overline B,-\overline A),\quad Q^I_\alpha{}^*=\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\quad \bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}{}^*=Q^I_\alpha,\quad T_{\alpha\dot\beta}^*=T_{\beta\dot\alpha},\quad (Z^{IJ})^*=\bar Z_{IJ},\quad (\bar Z_{IJ})^*=Z^{IJ}.$$

It uses the operator-adjoint convention $[x,y]^*=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[x^*,y^*]$. The associated real Lie superalgebra is the fixed space of the conjugate-linear map $\tau(x)=-x^*$ on even elements and $\tau(x)=i x^*$ on odd elements. Its real Lorentz algebra is the fixed diagonal copy of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$; its real translation generators are the $\tau$-fixed skew-Hermitian bispinors. The star-fixed translation coordinates defined below are abstract elements of the complex algebra; their multiples by $i$ form a real basis of the tau-fixed translation space.

For the metric convention $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, put $\sigma^0=I_2$ and

$$\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \bar\sigma^0=I_2,\qquad \bar\sigma^j=-\sigma^j.$$

They obey

$$\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu+\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu=-2\eta^{\mu\nu}I_2.$$

Define abstract translation coordinates $p_0=(T_{1\dot1}+T_{2\dot2})/2$, $p_1=(T_{1\dot2}+T_{2\dot1})/2$, $p_2=(T_{2\dot1}-T_{1\dot2})/(2i)$, and $p_3=(T_{1\dot1}-T_{2\dot2})/2$. Then $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}p_\mu$, $p_\mu^*=p_\mu$, and $\tau(ip_\mu)=ip_\mu$. A representation of the complex supertranslation algebra $\mathfrak t=V\oplus C_N\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$ on a graded complex vector space $\mathcal D$ means a parity-preserving complex-linear map $\rho:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$ preserving the bracket, where the target bracket on homogeneous endomorphisms is $[X,Y]=XY-(-1)^{|X||Y|}YX$. Write $P_\mu=\rho(p_\mu)$ and use the charge symbols for their images. Thus $\rho(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu$ and the represented mixed relation is $\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J$, with $P_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}P^\nu$. Complex linearity gives $\rho(ip_\mu)=iP_\mu$, hence $-i\rho(ip_\mu)=P_\mu$. For a real number $M>0$, a massive rest module here means such a supertranslation representation with $P^0=M I_{\mathcal D}$ and $P^j=0$ for $j=1,2,3$. Consequently $P_0=-M I_{\mathcal D}$ and its mixed anticommutator is $2M\delta_{\alpha\dot\beta}\delta^I{}_J I_{\mathcal D}$. This is an algebraic specialization, with no assertion of a Hilbert adjoint or a spectral fiber. Here $N$ counts left Weyl spinors; the scalar central-charge matrix is antisymmetric and therefore vanishes for $N=1$. Tensorial or topological extensions are outside this scalar-central-charge algebra. The convention uses natural units $\hbar=c=1$; translation and central-charge generators have mass dimension one and supercharges have mass dimension one-half.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

derivations.claim: The matrix commutators are antisymmetric and the odd-odd brackets are symmetric under interchange of the full generator labels: for the same-chirality bracket, $\epsilon_{\beta\alpha}Z^{JI}=(-\epsilon_{\alpha\beta})(-Z^{IJ})=\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ}$, and the dotted case is identical. The mixed bracket is symmetric by its Kronecker delta and the graded-skew rule. Each listed bracket has parity equal to the sum of its input parities, so the bracket is degree-preserving and graded-skew.

For matrices $X,Y,Z$, both $X(YZ-ZY)-(YZ-ZY)X$ and $(XY-YX)Z-Z(XY-YX)+Y(XZ-ZX)-(XZ-ZX)Y$ expand to $XYZ-XZY-YZX+ZYX$, so the commutator on $\mathfrak l$ satisfies Jacobi. Write $\rho_V(A,B)=A\otimes I+I\otimes B$. Operators acting on different tensor factors commute, hence $[\rho_V(A,B),\rho_V(A',B')]=[A,A']\otimes I+I\otimes[B,B']=\rho_V([(A,B),(A',B')])$. For the odd action, [F1] uses column entries: $[A,Q^I_\alpha]=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}Q^I_\gamma$. Consequently $[A,[A',Q^I_\alpha]]-[A',[A,Q^I_\alpha]]=\sum_\delta(AA'-A'A)^\delta{}_{\alpha}Q^I_\delta=[\, [A,A'],Q^I_\alpha]$, and the identical calculation applies to the dotted action of $B$. In particular, for $A=E_{12}$, $A'=E_{21}$ and $q=Q^I_1$, one has $[A,q]=0$, $[A',q]=Q^I_2$, and both sides of this identity are $q$. The actions on $C_N$ and by $V$ are zero. Thus $\mathfrak l$ acts by representations on the abelian space $V\oplus C_N$ and on $\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$; expanding the even Jacobi identity leaves precisely these representation identities, while brackets internal to $V\oplus C_N$ vanish.

For two even inputs and one odd input, the Jacobi expression is $[\rho(L),\rho(L')]q-\rho([L,L'])q$, which is zero by the fundamental-action identities in [F1]; if either even input lies in $V\oplus C_N$, its odd action is zero and the same expression vanishes. This checks all orderings of the two-even/one-odd case by graded skew-symmetry.

For one even input $L=(A,B)$ and two odd inputs, Jacobi is equivariance of their odd bracket. On a mixed pair, the two fundamental actions on $Q$ and $\bar Q$ give exactly $A\otimes I+I\otimes B$ on $T$, so the mixed bracket is equivariant. On an equal-chirality pair, writing $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{pmatrix}$ gives $A^{\mathsf T}\epsilon+\epsilon A=0$ by direct multiplication; the identical calculation for $B$ preserves the dotted alternating form. The flavor tensors $Z^{IJ}$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ are Lorentz scalars, so both central brackets are equivariant. Even inputs from $V\oplus C_N$ act trivially on each side.

The given star squares to the identity on each generator. On the matrix-commutator bracket, entrywise conjugation preserves matrix multiplication and the minus signs in $(A,B)^*$ reverse the bracket; on the fundamental and tensor actions, star exchanges the two spinor factors and the corresponding minus sign gives $[x,y]^*=-[x^*,y^*]$. On odd-odd brackets, star exchanges $Q$ with $\bar Q$, transposes the bispinor indices of $T$, and exchanges $Z$ with $\bar Z$; the real alternating-form coefficients and antisymmetric flavor labels give $[x,y]^*=[x^*,y^*]$, as required for two odd inputs. Zero brackets remain zero. For homogeneous even-even, even-odd and odd-odd inputs, substituting these identities into $\tau=-*$, $i*$ and $-*$ respectively gives $\tau([x,y])=[\tau x,\tau y]$; conjugate-linearity gives $\tau^2=I$. Therefore the fixed space is closed under the bracket. Every $x$ decomposes as $x_+ + i x_-$ with $x_+=(x+\tau x)/2$ and $x_-=(x-\tau x)/(2i)$ fixed by $\tau$, so this fixed real algebra complexifies to the displayed graded algebra.

For three odd inputs, each inner bracket lies in $V\oplus C_N$. Both summands act trivially on the odd space, so each of the three terms in the odd-odd-odd super-Jacobi identity is zero. The four parity patterns checked in the preceding cases exhaust homogeneous triples, and multilinearity gives the identity for arbitrary triples.
Pauli anticommutation and trace identities verify the temporal, mixed, and spatial cases of the sigma identity; direct matrix multiplication gives the displayed square and determinant formulas.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the complex Hilbert-space convention that the inner product is linear in its first variable and conjugate-linear in its second. Let $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\sigma^0=I_2$, $\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Define $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)=\{H\in M_2(\mathbb C):H^\dagger=H\}$ and $\Phi:\mathbb R^{1,3}\to\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$ by $\Phi(x)=-\sigma^\mu x_\mu$. For $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)=\{g\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det g=1\}$, define $\Lambda_g$ by $\Phi(\Lambda_gx)=g\Phi(x)g^\dagger$; the real-linear map $\Phi$ is an isomorphism because $I_2,\sigma^1,\sigma^2,\sigma^3$ form a basis of $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$. Since $\det g=1$, $\det(g\Phi(x)g^\dagger)=\det g\,\det\Phi(x)\,\overline{\det g}=\det\Phi(x)$; with $\det\Phi(x)=-\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu$, this proves determinant and Lorentz-form preservation. These maps satisfy $\Lambda_{I_2}=I$ and $\Lambda_g\Lambda_h=\Lambda_{gh}$: applying $\Phi$ to the left side gives $gh\Phi(x)h^\dagger g^\dagger=(gh)\Phi(x)(gh)^\dagger$, and injectivity of $\Phi$ gives the equality; in particular $\Lambda_{g^{-1}}=\Lambda_g^{-1}$. Thus $g\mapsto\Lambda_g$ is a group action, so it defines the semidirect-product structure below. Congruence by $g$ preserves positive-semidefinite Hermitian matrices, so $\Lambda_g$ preserves the chosen future cone. Let $\Lambda_g^\vee$ be the dual action on covectors, $(\Lambda_g^\vee p)(x)=p(\Lambda_g^{-1}x)$. The spin-cover Poincare group is $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with product $(g,a)(h,b)=(gh,a+\Lambda_gb)$.

A **positive unitary super-Poincare representation** in this item is the following data. It includes a nonzero complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and a bounded self-adjoint grading operator $\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^2=I$; write $\mathcal H^\pm=\ker(\Gamma\mp I)$. Give $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ the product topology from the usual matrix topology and Euclidean topology. Let $\mathcal U(\mathcal H)=\{V\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H):V^*V=VV^*=I\}$. The data include a map $U:\mathcal P\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H)$ satisfying $U(1,0)=I$ and $U((g,a)(h,b))=U(g,a)U(h,b)$ for all $(g,a),(h,b)\in\mathcal P$, with $U(g,a)\Gamma=\Gamma U(g,a)$. Require the orbit map $(g,a)\mapsto U(g,a)\psi$ to be norm-continuous for every $\psi\in\mathcal H$; this is strong continuity. The data also include a regular projection-valued measure $E$ on the Borel subsets of the covector space $(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ such that

$$U(1,a)=\Phi_E(p\mapsto e^{i p(a)}),\qquad U(g,0)E(B)U(g,0)^*=E(\Lambda_g^\vee B),\qquad E(\mathcal C_+^*)=I,$$

where $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral, $\mathcal C_+^*=\{p:p^0=-p_0\ge |\vec p|\}$ is the closed future cone in covector coordinates, and $p(a)=p_\mu a^\mu$. The PVM functional calculus makes every translation unitary commute with every $E(B)$. For each coordinate define the self-adjoint translation generator

$$P_\mu=p_\mu(E),\qquad D(P_\mu)=\left\{\psi\in\mathcal H:\int |p_\mu|^2\,dE_\psi(p)<\infty\right\},\qquad E_\psi(B)=\langle E(B)\psi,\psi\rangle.$$

Here $p_\mu(E)$ is the unbounded PVM integral with its truncation domain; the real-valued integral is self-adjoint under Countable Choice. Thus $P^0=\eta^{0\nu}P_\nu$ is nonnegative. The joint PVM is part of the representation data; no joint spectral measure is inferred from formal commutators on a dense domain.

For each $I,\alpha$, the supercharge $Q^I_\alpha$ is a closed densely defined operator on $\mathcal H$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ is its actual Hilbert adjoint, with exactly the adjoint domain. Require the grading to preserve each actual charge domain and each closed charge to be odd there: $\Gamma D(Q^I_\alpha)=D(Q^I_\alpha)$ and $Q^I_\alpha\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q^I_\alpha\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q^I_\alpha)$, with the same two conditions for $(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ on $D((Q^I_\alpha)^*)$. The central generators $Z^{IJ}$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$, which belong to the even part of the algebra, are represented by closed densely defined operators with $\bar Z_{IJ}=(Z^{IJ})^*$ as an actual Hilbert adjoint; require $\Gamma D(Z^{IJ})=D(Z^{IJ})$ and $Z^{IJ}\Gamma\psi=\Gamma Z^{IJ}\psi$ on $D(Z^{IJ})$, with the corresponding conditions for $\bar Z_{IJ}$ on its actual domain. On a common dense graded linear domain $\mathcal D$, contained in the domains of every generator product in the bracket table, the operator supercommutator is the displayed algebra bracket. In particular,

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J,\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

The domain $\mathcal D$ is invariant under those generators and under $U(\mathcal P)$. Explicitly, these restrictions define the complex-linear supertranslation representation $\rho_{\mathcal D}:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$: it sends the abstract $p_\mu$ to $P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$ and each abstract supercharge or central generator to its named operator restricted to $\mathcal D$. Invariance of $\mathcal D$ makes these endomorphisms, and the assumed bracket identities make $\rho_{\mathcal D}$ bracket-preserving. In particular, $\rho_{\mathcal D}(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$ and $-i\rho_{\mathcal D}(ip_\mu)=P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$. The even group acts on the charge domains exactly: for every $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)$, conjugation by $U(g,0)$ sends each closed charge to the corresponding fundamental or dotted spinor transform as an equality of operators, including equality of domains. The central generators transform as Lorentz scalars, commute with translations, and commute on $\mathcal D$ with all supercharges; these relations also include their domain invariance.

For every Borel set $B\subseteq(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ and every charge $Q$ or $Q^*$, require the reducing-projection/domain conditions

$$E(B)D(Q)\subseteq D(Q),\qquad Q E(B)\psi=E(B)Q\psi\quad(\psi\in D(Q)),$$

and the same conditions with $Q^*$ in place of $Q$. Require also $\Gamma E(B)=E(B)\Gamma$ for every Borel $B$. In particular this supplies integrated translation covariance with domain invariance; a relation $[P_\mu,Q]=0$ on a common core alone is not substituted for it. A closed complex-linear subspace $K$ is graded when $\Gamma K=K$, equivalently $K=(K\cap\mathcal H^+)\oplus(K\cap\mathcal H^-)$. Such a subspace is invariant when $U(g,a)K=K$ for all $(g,a)\in\mathcal P$ and each charge and adjoint maps $D(Q)\cap K$ into $K$, with those intersections dense in $K$. The representation is irreducible when its only such invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with The reals form a totally ordered field,
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).

derivations.claim: The function $s(p)=-\eta^{\mu\nu}p_\mu p_\nu=(p^0)^2-|\vec p|^2$ is continuous and nonnegative on the closed future cone in [F1]. For each Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$, $\{p\in\mathcal C_+^*:s(p)\in A\}$ is Borel in the full covector space because $\mathcal C_+^*$ is closed and $s$ is continuous there. Inverse images preserve disjoint unions, and the preimage of $[0,\infty)$ is $\mathcal C_+^*$, whose projection is $I$ by [F1]; therefore the pushforward $F(A):=E(\{p\in\mathcal C_+^*:s(p)\in A\})$ is a normalized PVM on $[0,\infty)$ by strong countable additivity of $E$.

For each Borel $A$, $F(A)$ is the projection $E(\{p\in\mathcal C_+^*:s(p)\in A\})$. The charge-domain reduction in [F1] therefore gives $F(A)D(Q)\subseteq D(Q)$ and $QF(A)\psi=F(A)Q\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q)$; the same argument applies to $Q^*$. This proves the spectral-subspace assertion.

The determinant formula in [F1] and $\det g=1$ give $\det\Phi(\Lambda_gx)=\det(g\Phi(x)g^\dagger)=\det\Phi(x)$, hence $\eta_{\mu
u}(\Lambda_gx)^\mu(\Lambda_gx)^
u=\eta_{\mu
u}x^\mu x^
u$. Polarization of this quadratic identity gives $\Lambda_g^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda_g=\eta$. By the dual-action definition in [F1], a covector column transforms as $(\Lambda_g^{-1})^{\mathsf T}p$; the inverse-metric identity $\Lambda_g^{-1}\eta^{-1}(\Lambda_g^{-1})^{\mathsf T}=\eta^{-1}$ therefore gives $s(\Lambda_g^\vee p)=s(p)$. Under the metric identification $p^\sharp=\eta^{-1}p$, this dual action satisfies $(\Lambda_g^\vee p)^\sharp=\Lambda_g p^\sharp$; preservation of the future vector cone therefore gives preservation of $\mathcal C_+^*$. Lorentz covariance of $E$ now implies $U(g,0)F(A)U(g,0)^*=F(A)$. Translation unitaries are bounded Borel functions of $E$, so they commute with every $F(A)$; $\Gamma$ commutes with $E$ by [F1]. Hence $\operatorname{ran}F(A)$ is closed and graded, invariant under the integrated even group, and invariant under every charge and adjoint with dense restricted domains: density follows by applying the bounded projection $F(A)$ to a dense operator domain. Irreducibility as defined in [F1] forces $F(A)=0$ or $F(A)=I$.

Choose any nonzero vector and normalize it to a unit vector $\psi\in\mathcal H$; set $\mu(A)=\langle F(A)\psi,\psi\rangle$. By [F3] this is a countably additive probability measure, and by step 2.2 every value is $0$ or $1$. For any measurable sets $A_n$, define disjoint $C_n=A_n\setminus\bigcup_{k<n}A_k$. If $C\subseteq A$, countable additivity on $A=C\sqcup(A\setminus C)$ gives $\mu(C)\le\mu(A)$; hence $\mu(\bigcup_n A_n)=\sum_n\mu(C_n)\le\sum_n\mu(A_n)$. Thus countable subadditivity is available here from countable additivity and nonnegativity, without an additional supplier. The set $R=\{r\ge0:\mu([0,r])=1\}$ is nonempty: otherwise countable subadditivity applied to $[0,\infty)=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[0,n]$ would give $\mu([0,\infty))=0$, contradicting that $\mu$ is a probability measure. Put $m^2=\inf R$, which is a finite nonnegative real.

For every $\varepsilon>0$, the infimum property gives $r\in R$ with $r<m^2+\varepsilon$, so $\mu([0,m^2+\varepsilon])=1$. If $m^2>\varepsilon$, then $m^2-\varepsilon<m^2$ is not in $R$, and the zero-or-one property gives $\mu([0,m^2-\varepsilon])=0$. Thus for all sufficiently large $n$, the nested intervals $I_n=(\max(0,m^2-1/n),m^2+1/n]$ have measure one; when $m^2=0$, use $I_n=[0,1/n]$. Here is the needed continuity-from-above argument. If $(D_n)_{n\ge n_0}$ is any decreasing sequence of measurable sets with $\mu(D_{n_0})<\infty$, put $C_n=D_n\setminus D_{n+1}$. Then the $C_n$ are disjoint and $D_k=(\bigcap_{n\ge n_0}D_n)\sqcup\bigcup_{n\ge k}C_n$ for each $k\ge n_0$. Countable additivity gives $\mu(D_k)=\mu(\bigcap_{n\ge n_0}D_n)+\sum_{n\ge k}\mu(C_n)$. Since $\bigcup_{n\ge n_0}C_n\subseteq D_{n_0}$, monotonicity of $\mu$ from step 3.1 bounds the series by $\mu(D_{n_0})<\infty$; its tails therefore tend to zero. Thus $\lim_k\mu(D_k)=\mu(\bigcap_{n\ge n_0}D_n)$. Apply this to the tail $(I_n)_{n\ge n_0}$ on which $\mu(I_n)=1$; its intersection is $\{m^2\}$, so $\mu(\{m^2\})=\lim_{n\ge n_0}\mu(I_n)=1$. Therefore $F(\{m^2\})\ne0$, and step 2.2 forces $F(\{m^2\})=I$. If $A$ contains $m^2$, monotonicity gives $F(A)=I$; if not, then $\mu(A)=0$ because $A$ is disjoint from $\{m^2\}$, so the zero-or-one property gives $F(A)=0$. This rule also proves uniqueness: any second value with projection $I$ would have to equal $m^2$, since the singleton projections for distinct values are orthogonal.

By [F4], $m^2$ has a unique nonnegative square root $m$. Step 2.1 shows that each charge maps vectors in a fixed mass-squared subspace into that same subspace; step 4.1 shows there is only one such spectral value in the irreducible representation. The argument uses the pushforward PVM rather than a normalizable sharp-momentum vector, and it includes $m=0$ without introducing a rest frame.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Use the complex field $\mathbb C$ with conjugation $z\mapsto\overline z$. Fix an integer $N\ge1$. Let $S=\mathbb C^2$ have standard basis $s_1,s_2$. For a complex vector space $W$, its conjugate vector space $\overline W$ consists of symbols $\overline w$ for $w\in W$, with addition $\overline w+\overline v=\overline{w+v}$ and scalar action $\lambda\overline w=\overline{\overline\lambda w}$. Set $\dot S=\overline S$ with dotted basis $\dot s_{\dot1}=\overline{s_1}$ and $\dot s_{\dot2}=\overline{s_2}$. Let $F=\mathbb C^N$ have standard basis $f_1,\ldots,f_N$, and let $F^*$ be its complex-linear dual with dual basis $f^1,\ldots,f^N$ and scalar action $(\lambda\ell)(v)=\lambda\ell(v)$. All tensor products are over $\mathbb C$, with scalar action $\lambda(v\otimes w)=(\lambda v)\otimes w=v\otimes(\lambda w)$ and product bases formed from the displayed bases. Define $\Lambda^2F=(F\otimes_{\mathbb C}F)/\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{v\otimes v:v\in F\}$; its basis is $f_I\wedge f_J$ for $1\le I<J\le N$, with quotient scalar action. Its conjugate $\overline{\Lambda^2F}$ has basis $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ and the conjugate scalar action just defined. For $N=1$ these exterior-square spaces are zero. In the displayed bases, $\mathfrak{sl}(S)=\{A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(S):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$ and $\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)=\{B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\dot S):\operatorname{tr}B=0\}$. Put $\epsilon_{12}=\epsilon_{\dot1\dot2}=1$ and $\epsilon_{21}=\epsilon_{\dot2\dot1}=-1$, with zero diagonal. The complex even space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar0}=\bigl(\mathfrak{sl}(S)\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)\bigr)\oplus V\oplus C_N,\qquad V=S\otimes\dot S,\qquad C_N=\Lambda^2F\oplus\overline{\Lambda^2F}.$$

Write $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=s_\alpha\otimes\dot s_{\dot\beta}$ for the basis of $V$. The listed central generators form a basis of $C_N$: $Z^{IJ}$ corresponds to $f_I\wedge f_J$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ to $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ for $1\le I<J\le N$; extend them by antisymmetry in the flavor indices and set their diagonal entries to zero. The complex odd space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar1}=(S\otimes F)\oplus(\dot S\otimes F^*),$$

with basis $Q^I_\alpha=s_\alpha\otimes f_I$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=\dot s_{\dot\alpha}\otimes f^I$. A homogeneous vector has parity $|x|\in\{0,1\}$. The bracket is complex-bilinear, preserves parity, and obeys $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$. Its complete nonzero table, apart from the graded-skew consequences, is

$$[ (A,B),(A',B') ]=([A,A'],[B,B']),\qquad [(A,B),T]= (A\otimes I+I\otimes B)T,$$

$$[(A,B),Q^I_\alpha]=A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}Q^I_\gamma,\qquad [(A,B),\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}]=B^{\dot\gamma}{}_{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\gamma I},$$

Here $A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}$ is the entry in row $\gamma$, column $\alpha$, so $As_\alpha=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}s_\gamma$; dotted entries use the same convention. Thus on the translation basis the tensor action is $[(A,B),T_{\alpha\dot\beta}]=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}T_{\gamma\dot\beta}+\sum_{\dot\gamma}B^{\dot\gamma}{}_{\dot\beta}T_{\alpha\dot\gamma}$.

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\delta^I{}_J T_{\alpha\dot\beta},\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

All other brackets vanish: $V$ and $C_N$ are abelian, $C_N$ is central, and $V$ brackets trivially with the odd space. The two antisymmetric factors in each equal-chirality odd bracket make that bracket symmetric in the combined spinor-flavor labels. The Lie-superalgebra and real-form properties are established by the local Jacobi result.

Define a conjugate-linear involution $*$ on the generators by

$$ (A,B)^*=(-\overline B,-\overline A),\quad Q^I_\alpha{}^*=\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\quad \bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}{}^*=Q^I_\alpha,\quad T_{\alpha\dot\beta}^*=T_{\beta\dot\alpha},\quad (Z^{IJ})^*=\bar Z_{IJ},\quad (\bar Z_{IJ})^*=Z^{IJ}.$$

It uses the operator-adjoint convention $[x,y]^*=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[x^*,y^*]$. The associated real Lie superalgebra is the fixed space of the conjugate-linear map $\tau(x)=-x^*$ on even elements and $\tau(x)=i x^*$ on odd elements. Its real Lorentz algebra is the fixed diagonal copy of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$; its real translation generators are the $\tau$-fixed skew-Hermitian bispinors. The star-fixed translation coordinates defined below are abstract elements of the complex algebra; their multiples by $i$ form a real basis of the tau-fixed translation space.

For the metric convention $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, put $\sigma^0=I_2$ and

$$\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \bar\sigma^0=I_2,\qquad \bar\sigma^j=-\sigma^j.$$

They obey

$$\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu+\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu=-2\eta^{\mu\nu}I_2.$$

Define abstract translation coordinates $p_0=(T_{1\dot1}+T_{2\dot2})/2$, $p_1=(T_{1\dot2}+T_{2\dot1})/2$, $p_2=(T_{2\dot1}-T_{1\dot2})/(2i)$, and $p_3=(T_{1\dot1}-T_{2\dot2})/2$. Then $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}p_\mu$, $p_\mu^*=p_\mu$, and $\tau(ip_\mu)=ip_\mu$. A representation of the complex supertranslation algebra $\mathfrak t=V\oplus C_N\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$ on a graded complex vector space $\mathcal D$ means a parity-preserving complex-linear map $\rho:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$ preserving the bracket, where the target bracket on homogeneous endomorphisms is $[X,Y]=XY-(-1)^{|X||Y|}YX$. Write $P_\mu=\rho(p_\mu)$ and use the charge symbols for their images. Thus $\rho(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu$ and the represented mixed relation is $\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J$, with $P_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}P^\nu$. Complex linearity gives $\rho(ip_\mu)=iP_\mu$, hence $-i\rho(ip_\mu)=P_\mu$. For a real number $M>0$, a massive rest module here means such a supertranslation representation with $P^0=M I_{\mathcal D}$ and $P^j=0$ for $j=1,2,3$. Consequently $P_0=-M I_{\mathcal D}$ and its mixed anticommutator is $2M\delta_{\alpha\dot\beta}\delta^I{}_J I_{\mathcal D}$. This is an algebraic specialization, with no assertion of a Hilbert adjoint or a spectral fiber. Here $N$ counts left Weyl spinors; the scalar central-charge matrix is antisymmetric and therefore vanishes for $N=1$. Tensorial or topological extensions are outside this scalar-central-charge algebra. The convention uses natural units $\hbar=c=1$; translation and central-charge generators have mass dimension one and supercharges have mass dimension one-half.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the complex Hilbert-space convention that the inner product is linear in its first variable and conjugate-linear in its second. Let $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\sigma^0=I_2$, $\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Define $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)=\{H\in M_2(\mathbb C):H^\dagger=H\}$ and $\Phi:\mathbb R^{1,3}\to\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$ by $\Phi(x)=-\sigma^\mu x_\mu$. For $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)=\{g\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det g=1\}$, define $\Lambda_g$ by $\Phi(\Lambda_gx)=g\Phi(x)g^\dagger$; the real-linear map $\Phi$ is an isomorphism because $I_2,\sigma^1,\sigma^2,\sigma^3$ form a basis of $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$. Since $\det g=1$, $\det(g\Phi(x)g^\dagger)=\det g\,\det\Phi(x)\,\overline{\det g}=\det\Phi(x)$; with $\det\Phi(x)=-\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu$, this proves determinant and Lorentz-form preservation. These maps satisfy $\Lambda_{I_2}=I$ and $\Lambda_g\Lambda_h=\Lambda_{gh}$: applying $\Phi$ to the left side gives $gh\Phi(x)h^\dagger g^\dagger=(gh)\Phi(x)(gh)^\dagger$, and injectivity of $\Phi$ gives the equality; in particular $\Lambda_{g^{-1}}=\Lambda_g^{-1}$. Thus $g\mapsto\Lambda_g$ is a group action, so it defines the semidirect-product structure below. Congruence by $g$ preserves positive-semidefinite Hermitian matrices, so $\Lambda_g$ preserves the chosen future cone. Let $\Lambda_g^\vee$ be the dual action on covectors, $(\Lambda_g^\vee p)(x)=p(\Lambda_g^{-1}x)$. The spin-cover Poincare group is $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with product $(g,a)(h,b)=(gh,a+\Lambda_gb)$.

A **positive unitary super-Poincare representation** in this item is the following data. It includes a nonzero complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and a bounded self-adjoint grading operator $\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^2=I$; write $\mathcal H^\pm=\ker(\Gamma\mp I)$. Give $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ the product topology from the usual matrix topology and Euclidean topology. Let $\mathcal U(\mathcal H)=\{V\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H):V^*V=VV^*=I\}$. The data include a map $U:\mathcal P\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H)$ satisfying $U(1,0)=I$ and $U((g,a)(h,b))=U(g,a)U(h,b)$ for all $(g,a),(h,b)\in\mathcal P$, with $U(g,a)\Gamma=\Gamma U(g,a)$. Require the orbit map $(g,a)\mapsto U(g,a)\psi$ to be norm-continuous for every $\psi\in\mathcal H$; this is strong continuity. The data also include a regular projection-valued measure $E$ on the Borel subsets of the covector space $(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ such that

$$U(1,a)=\Phi_E(p\mapsto e^{i p(a)}),\qquad U(g,0)E(B)U(g,0)^*=E(\Lambda_g^\vee B),\qquad E(\mathcal C_+^*)=I,$$

where $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral, $\mathcal C_+^*=\{p:p^0=-p_0\ge |\vec p|\}$ is the closed future cone in covector coordinates, and $p(a)=p_\mu a^\mu$. The PVM functional calculus makes every translation unitary commute with every $E(B)$. For each coordinate define the self-adjoint translation generator

$$P_\mu=p_\mu(E),\qquad D(P_\mu)=\left\{\psi\in\mathcal H:\int |p_\mu|^2\,dE_\psi(p)<\infty\right\},\qquad E_\psi(B)=\langle E(B)\psi,\psi\rangle.$$

Here $p_\mu(E)$ is the unbounded PVM integral with its truncation domain; the real-valued integral is self-adjoint under Countable Choice. Thus $P^0=\eta^{0\nu}P_\nu$ is nonnegative. The joint PVM is part of the representation data; no joint spectral measure is inferred from formal commutators on a dense domain.

For each $I,\alpha$, the supercharge $Q^I_\alpha$ is a closed densely defined operator on $\mathcal H$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ is its actual Hilbert adjoint, with exactly the adjoint domain. Require the grading to preserve each actual charge domain and each closed charge to be odd there: $\Gamma D(Q^I_\alpha)=D(Q^I_\alpha)$ and $Q^I_\alpha\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q^I_\alpha\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q^I_\alpha)$, with the same two conditions for $(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ on $D((Q^I_\alpha)^*)$. The central generators $Z^{IJ}$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$, which belong to the even part of the algebra, are represented by closed densely defined operators with $\bar Z_{IJ}=(Z^{IJ})^*$ as an actual Hilbert adjoint; require $\Gamma D(Z^{IJ})=D(Z^{IJ})$ and $Z^{IJ}\Gamma\psi=\Gamma Z^{IJ}\psi$ on $D(Z^{IJ})$, with the corresponding conditions for $\bar Z_{IJ}$ on its actual domain. On a common dense graded linear domain $\mathcal D$, contained in the domains of every generator product in the bracket table, the operator supercommutator is the displayed algebra bracket. In particular,

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J,\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

The domain $\mathcal D$ is invariant under those generators and under $U(\mathcal P)$. Explicitly, these restrictions define the complex-linear supertranslation representation $\rho_{\mathcal D}:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$: it sends the abstract $p_\mu$ to $P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$ and each abstract supercharge or central generator to its named operator restricted to $\mathcal D$. Invariance of $\mathcal D$ makes these endomorphisms, and the assumed bracket identities make $\rho_{\mathcal D}$ bracket-preserving. In particular, $\rho_{\mathcal D}(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$ and $-i\rho_{\mathcal D}(ip_\mu)=P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$. The even group acts on the charge domains exactly: for every $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)$, conjugation by $U(g,0)$ sends each closed charge to the corresponding fundamental or dotted spinor transform as an equality of operators, including equality of domains. The central generators transform as Lorentz scalars, commute with translations, and commute on $\mathcal D$ with all supercharges; these relations also include their domain invariance.

For every Borel set $B\subseteq(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ and every charge $Q$ or $Q^*$, require the reducing-projection/domain conditions

$$E(B)D(Q)\subseteq D(Q),\qquad Q E(B)\psi=E(B)Q\psi\quad(\psi\in D(Q)),$$

and the same conditions with $Q^*$ in place of $Q$. Require also $\Gamma E(B)=E(B)\Gamma$ for every Borel $B$. In particular this supplies integrated translation covariance with domain invariance; a relation $[P_\mu,Q]=0$ on a common core alone is not substituted for it. A closed complex-linear subspace $K$ is graded when $\Gamma K=K$, equivalently $K=(K\cap\mathcal H^+)\oplus(K\cap\mathcal H^-)$. Such a subspace is invariant when $U(g,a)K=K$ for all $(g,a)\in\mathcal P$ and each charge and adjoint maps $D(Q)\cap K$ into $K$, with those intersections dense in $K$. The representation is irreducible when its only such invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

inner product linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$
so that $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$
onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

derivations.claim: If $\psi\in E_\lambda$, then $\psi\in D(Q)$, $Q\psi\in D(Q)$ and $Q^2\psi=\lambda\psi$ by [F3]. Thus $Q\psi\in D(Q)$ and $Q(Q\psi)=\lambda\psi\in D(Q)$, so a second application of [F3] gives $Q\psi\in D(H)$. Moreover $H(Q\psi)=Q(Q^2\psi)=Q(\lambda\psi)=\lambda Q\psi$. Therefore $Q$ maps $E_\lambda$ into itself.

The domain of $H$ is invariant under $\Gamma$: if $\psi\in D(H)$, then $\Gamma\psi\in D(Q)$ by hypothesis and $Q\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q\psi\in D(Q)$ because $Q\psi\in D(Q)$ and $D(Q)$ is $\Gamma$-invariant. Applying the anticommutation relation twice gives $H\Gamma\psi=\Gamma H\psi$. Hence $\Gamma E_\lambda=E_\lambda$, and $Q\Gamma=-\Gamma Q$ shows that $Q$ maps $E_\lambda^+$ to $E_\lambda^-$ and $E_\lambda^-$ to $E_\lambda^+$.

For $\psi,\varphi\in E_\lambda$, both vectors lie in $D(Q)$ and $Q\psi\in D(Q)$, by [F2], the adjoint is taken in the complete Hilbert space; self-adjointness in [F5] and the identity in [F4] give $\langle Q\psi,Q\varphi\rangle=\langle Q^2\psi,\varphi\rangle=\lambda\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle$. By [F6], and since $\sqrt\lambda$ is nonzero in the complex field by [F7], division by $\sqrt\lambda$ therefore makes $Q$ an isometry on $E_\lambda$. Also $(Q/\sqrt\lambda)^2\psi=Q^2\psi/\lambda=\psi$ there. Together with the parity exchange in step 2.1, this proves that the restriction $U_\lambda:E_\lambda^+\to E_\lambda^-$ is an isometry with inverse the restriction from $E_\lambda^-$ to $E_\lambda^+$; it is consequently unitary and the finite dimensions agree.

If $\psi\in\ker H$, then $\psi\in D(Q^2)$, so $Q\psi\in D(Q)$. By [F2], [F5] and the adjoint identity [F4], $\|Q\psi\|^2=\langle Q\psi,Q\psi\rangle=\langle Q^2\psi,\psi\rangle=0$. Positive definiteness in [F1] forces $Q\psi=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H=\mathcal H^+\oplus\mathcal H^-$ be a complex Hilbert space with grading operator $\Gamma=+I$ on $\mathcal H^+$ and $\Gamma=-I$ on $\mathcal H^-$. Let $Q$ be a densely defined self-adjoint operator with domain invariant under $\Gamma$ and $Q\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q)$. Set $H=Q^2$ on the composition domain $D(H)=\{\psi\in D(Q):Q\psi\in D(Q)\}$. For each $\lambda>0$, let $E_\lambda=\{\psi\in D(H):H\psi=\lambda\psi\}$ be finite-dimensional, and put $E_\lambda^\pm=E_\lambda\cap\mathcal H^\pm$. Then $Q$ maps $E_\lambda$ into itself, and

$$U_\lambda:=(Q/\sqrt{\lambda})|_{E_\lambda^+}:E_\lambda^+\longrightarrow E_\lambda^-$$

is a unitary isomorphism, with inverse $(Q/\sqrt{\lambda})|_{E_\lambda^-}$. In particular $\dim E_\lambda^+=\dim E_\lambda^-$. Also $Q\psi=0$ for every zero-energy vector $\psi\in\ker H$. No discrete spectrum or finite-multiplicity assumption is made about energies other than the selected $\lambda$.

A **pure-point graded trace-class index datum** consists of a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H=\mathcal H^+\oplus\mathcal H^-$, its grading operator $\Gamma$ equal to $+I$ on $\mathcal H^+$ and $-I$ on $\mathcal H^-$, and a densely defined self-adjoint operator $Q$ such that $D(Q)$ is invariant under $\Gamma$ and $Q\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q)$. Set $H=Q^2$ on $D(H)=\{\psi\in D(Q):Q\psi\in D(Q)\}$ and require this composition operator to be nonnegative and self-adjoint. Assume $H$ has the orthogonal pure-point decomposition

$$\mathcal H=\mathcal H_0^+\oplus\mathcal H_0^-\oplus\widehat{\bigoplus}_{\lambda\in\Sigma}(\mathcal H_\lambda^+\oplus\mathcal H_\lambda^-),$$

where $\Sigma\subset(0,\infty)$ is a supplied countable set of distinct eigenvalues, $\mathcal H_0^\pm=\ker H\cap\mathcal H^\pm$ are finite-dimensional, and $\mathcal H_\lambda^\pm=\ker(H-\lambda I)\cap\mathcal H^\pm$ are finite-dimensional eigenspaces contained in $D(H)$. Supply orthonormal bases of these subspaces whose union $E=E^+\sqcup E^-$ is a Hilbert basis of $\mathcal H$ compatible with energy and parity. Assume Countable Choice as used by the imported Hilbert-space, adjoint and trace-class definitions. The local positive-energy-pairing lemma derives, rather than assumes, the unitary map $Q/\sqrt\lambda:\mathcal H_\lambda^+\to\mathcal H_\lambda^-$ and equality of their finite dimensions.

For each real $\beta>0$, a bounded diagonal operator $T_\beta$ is supplied as part of the data, with $T_\beta e=e^{-\beta\lambda}e$ on $E_\lambda^+\cup E_\lambda^-$ and $T_\beta e=e$ on $E_0^+\cup E_0^-$. Require $T_\beta$ to be trace class for every $\beta>0$; it is denoted $e^{-\beta H}$. Its graded heat supertrace, called the **Witten index at parameter $\beta$** in this data class, is

$$W(\beta):=\sum_{e\in E^+}\langle T_\beta e,e\rangle-\sum_{e\in E^-}\langle T_\beta e,e\rangle,$$

where each family sum is in the finite-subset sense for absolutely summable scalar families. The supplied trace-class Hilbert-basis definition makes these sums absolutely convergent. Here $\beta$ is only a positive real mathematical parameter and has no assigned physical units or temperature interpretation. The index datum is discrete: it contains no continuous spectral subspace or continuum regularization prescription, and makes no physical model identification.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $Q/\sqrt\lambda$ is a linear bijection between the finite-dimensional positive-energy parity eigenspaces, so $m_\lambda^+:=\dim\mathcal H_\lambda^+=\dim\mathcal H_\lambda^-=:m_\lambda^-$ for every $\lambda\in\Sigma$. On any supplied orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_\lambda^\pm$, [F2] gives $\langle T_\beta e,e\rangle=e^{-\beta\lambda}$ for each basis vector. Therefore the positive-energy contribution to the signed basis sum at this fixed $\lambda$ is $e^{-\beta\lambda}(m_\lambda^+-m_\lambda^-)=0$.

By [F2], the full diagonal family is absolutely summable. For the partition into its energy blocks, the absolute value of each block sum is at most the sum of the absolute values in that block; hence the family of block sums is also absolutely summable. To see that its sum equals the original sum, fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose a finite set of basis vectors whose omitted absolute tail is below $\varepsilon$. Only finitely many energy blocks meet that finite set, and the omitted absolute tail bounds the difference between the full sum and the sum of those complete block sums. Letting $\varepsilon$ decrease to zero proves that grouping by energy preserves the sum. Step 1.1 cancels every positive-energy block; each zero-energy even basis vector contributes $1$ and each zero-energy odd basis vector contributes $-1$. The remaining finite sum is $m_0^+-m_0^-$, independent of $\beta$. The proof uses no trace cyclicity and no positive-energy eigenvector outside the given discrete decomposition.

Use the complex field $\mathbb C$ with conjugation $z\mapsto\overline z$. Fix an integer $N\ge1$. Let $S=\mathbb C^2$ have standard basis $s_1,s_2$. For a complex vector space $W$, its conjugate vector space $\overline W$ consists of symbols $\overline w$ for $w\in W$, with addition $\overline w+\overline v=\overline{w+v}$ and scalar action $\lambda\overline w=\overline{\overline\lambda w}$. Set $\dot S=\overline S$ with dotted basis $\dot s_{\dot1}=\overline{s_1}$ and $\dot s_{\dot2}=\overline{s_2}$. Let $F=\mathbb C^N$ have standard basis $f_1,\ldots,f_N$, and let $F^*$ be its complex-linear dual with dual basis $f^1,\ldots,f^N$ and scalar action $(\lambda\ell)(v)=\lambda\ell(v)$. All tensor products are over $\mathbb C$, with scalar action $\lambda(v\otimes w)=(\lambda v)\otimes w=v\otimes(\lambda w)$ and product bases formed from the displayed bases. Define $\Lambda^2F=(F\otimes_{\mathbb C}F)/\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{v\otimes v:v\in F\}$; its basis is $f_I\wedge f_J$ for $1\le I<J\le N$, with quotient scalar action. Its conjugate $\overline{\Lambda^2F}$ has basis $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ and the conjugate scalar action just defined. For $N=1$ these exterior-square spaces are zero. In the displayed bases, $\mathfrak{sl}(S)=\{A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(S):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$ and $\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)=\{B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\dot S):\operatorname{tr}B=0\}$. Put $\epsilon_{12}=\epsilon_{\dot1\dot2}=1$ and $\epsilon_{21}=\epsilon_{\dot2\dot1}=-1$, with zero diagonal. The complex even space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar0}=\bigl(\mathfrak{sl}(S)\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)\bigr)\oplus V\oplus C_N,\qquad V=S\otimes\dot S,\qquad C_N=\Lambda^2F\oplus\overline{\Lambda^2F}.$$

Write $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=s_\alpha\otimes\dot s_{\dot\beta}$ for the basis of $V$. The listed central generators form a basis of $C_N$: $Z^{IJ}$ corresponds to $f_I\wedge f_J$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ to $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ for $1\le I<J\le N$; extend them by antisymmetry in the flavor indices and set their diagonal entries to zero. The complex odd space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar1}=(S\otimes F)\oplus(\dot S\otimes F^*),$$

with basis $Q^I_\alpha=s_\alpha\otimes f_I$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=\dot s_{\dot\alpha}\otimes f^I$. A homogeneous vector has parity $|x|\in\{0,1\}$. The bracket is complex-bilinear, preserves parity, and obeys $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$. Its complete nonzero table, apart from the graded-skew consequences, is

$$[ (A,B),(A',B') ]=([A,A'],[B,B']),\qquad [(A,B),T]= (A\otimes I+I\otimes B)T,$$

$$[(A,B),Q^I_\alpha]=A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}Q^I_\gamma,\qquad [(A,B),\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}]=B^{\dot\gamma}{}_{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\gamma I},$$

Here $A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}$ is the entry in row $\gamma$, column $\alpha$, so $As_\alpha=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}s_\gamma$; dotted entries use the same convention. Thus on the translation basis the tensor action is $[(A,B),T_{\alpha\dot\beta}]=\sum_\gamma A^\gamma{}_{\alpha}T_{\gamma\dot\beta}+\sum_{\dot\gamma}B^{\dot\gamma}{}_{\dot\beta}T_{\alpha\dot\gamma}$.

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\delta^I{}_J T_{\alpha\dot\beta},\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

All other brackets vanish: $V$ and $C_N$ are abelian, $C_N$ is central, and $V$ brackets trivially with the odd space. The two antisymmetric factors in each equal-chirality odd bracket make that bracket symmetric in the combined spinor-flavor labels. The Lie-superalgebra and real-form properties are established by the local Jacobi result.

Define a conjugate-linear involution $*$ on the generators by

$$ (A,B)^*=(-\overline B,-\overline A),\quad Q^I_\alpha{}^*=\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\quad \bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}{}^*=Q^I_\alpha,\quad T_{\alpha\dot\beta}^*=T_{\beta\dot\alpha},\quad (Z^{IJ})^*=\bar Z_{IJ},\quad (\bar Z_{IJ})^*=Z^{IJ}.$$

It uses the operator-adjoint convention $[x,y]^*=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[x^*,y^*]$. The associated real Lie superalgebra is the fixed space of the conjugate-linear map $\tau(x)=-x^*$ on even elements and $\tau(x)=i x^*$ on odd elements. Its real Lorentz algebra is the fixed diagonal copy of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$; its real translation generators are the $\tau$-fixed skew-Hermitian bispinors. The star-fixed translation coordinates defined below are abstract elements of the complex algebra; their multiples by $i$ form a real basis of the tau-fixed translation space.

For the metric convention $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, put $\sigma^0=I_2$ and

$$\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \bar\sigma^0=I_2,\qquad \bar\sigma^j=-\sigma^j.$$

They obey

$$\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu+\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu=-2\eta^{\mu\nu}I_2.$$

Define abstract translation coordinates $p_0=(T_{1\dot1}+T_{2\dot2})/2$, $p_1=(T_{1\dot2}+T_{2\dot1})/2$, $p_2=(T_{2\dot1}-T_{1\dot2})/(2i)$, and $p_3=(T_{1\dot1}-T_{2\dot2})/2$. Then $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}p_\mu$, $p_\mu^*=p_\mu$, and $\tau(ip_\mu)=ip_\mu$. A representation of the complex supertranslation algebra $\mathfrak t=V\oplus C_N\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$ on a graded complex vector space $\mathcal D$ means a parity-preserving complex-linear map $\rho:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$ preserving the bracket, where the target bracket on homogeneous endomorphisms is $[X,Y]=XY-(-1)^{|X||Y|}YX$. Write $P_\mu=\rho(p_\mu)$ and use the charge symbols for their images. Thus $\rho(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu$ and the represented mixed relation is $\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J$, with $P_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}P^\nu$. Complex linearity gives $\rho(ip_\mu)=iP_\mu$, hence $-i\rho(ip_\mu)=P_\mu$. For a real number $M>0$, a massive rest module here means such a supertranslation representation with $P^0=M I_{\mathcal D}$ and $P^j=0$ for $j=1,2,3$. Consequently $P_0=-M I_{\mathcal D}$ and its mixed anticommutator is $2M\delta_{\alpha\dot\beta}\delta^I{}_J I_{\mathcal D}$. This is an algebraic specialization, with no assertion of a Hilbert adjoint or a spectral fiber. derivations.claim: The map $Q$ is a self-adjoint matrix on the displayed orthonormal basis: its only nonzero block in the ordered pair $(|b\rangle,|f\rangle)$ is $\sqrt\omega\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, a real symmetric matrix, and it is zero on the orthogonal zero-energy subspace. This block exchanges parity, and its square is $\omega I$; thus $H$ is $0$ on the three zero states and $\omega I$ on the positive pair. For each $\beta>0$, the supplied diagonal $T_\beta$ has eigenvalue $1$ on the zero states and $e^{-\beta\omega}$ on the positive pair, so it is exactly the operator denoted $e^{-\beta H}$ in [F1]. Its norm is $\max\{1,e^{-\beta\omega}\}<\infty$, so it is bounded; its five diagonal entries give finite rank, hence it is trace class by [F4] (equivalently, its singular values have finite sum $3+2e^{-\beta\omega}$). Thus the data satisfy the boundedness, trace-class and finite pure-point hypotheses for every $\beta>0$.

The three zero modes contribute $2-1=1$ to the supertrace. The positive pair contributes $e^{-\beta\omega}-e^{-\beta\omega}=0$, so direct evaluation gives $W(\beta)=1$. By [F2], this also equals $m_0^+-m_0^-=2-1$. This calculation is finite dimensional and makes no continuum or regularization claim.
